questions.q: How does an AWS service like Glue or Lambda actually get permission to call other AWS services?
options: It's configured with an execution role, which the service itself assumes at runtime, receiving temporary credentials from STS
AWS automatically embeds a permanent access key into every service's runtime environment
The service inherits whatever permissions the account root user has, with no configuration needed
Services cannot call other AWS services under any circumstances
questions.explain: Execution roles (or instance profiles for EC2) are assumed by the service at runtime, producing temporary, scoped credentials — no access key involved.

questions.q: In the trust policy example with Principal: {"Service": "glue.amazonaws.com"}, what does this statement actually allow?
options: Only the AWS Glue service is allowed to assume this specific role via sts:AssumeRole
Every AWS service in existence is allowed to assume this role
Only IAM users in the account named "glue" can log in
It grants Glue full administrator access to the entire account
questions.explain: A trust policy's Principal names exactly who or what can assume the role — here, specifically the Glue service and nothing else.

questions.q: What are the two separate policies that exist on a single IAM role, per this lesson?
options: A trust policy (who/what can assume the role) and a permissions policy (what the assumed role can actually do)
A billing policy and a networking policy
Two identical copies of the same permissions policy for redundancy
A role only ever has one policy, never two
questions.explain: The trust policy answers 'who can assume this,' while the permissions policy (covered in Lesson 12) answers 'what can it do once assumed.'

questions.q: In the cross-account access example, how does a user in Account A get temporary access to a role in Account B?
options: Account B's role has a trust policy naming Account A as a trusted Principal; the Account A user calls sts:AssumeRole and STS returns temporary credentials
Account A and Account B must be merged into a single AWS account first
Account B must create a permanent IAM user for the Account A person to log in as
Cross-account access is not possible in AWS under any configuration
questions.explain: This is the standard AWS cross-account pattern: a trust relationship plus sts:AssumeRole, with no standing user created in either account.

questions.q: Besides role assumption, what other pattern does this lesson describe for granting cross-service access?
options: A resource-based policy directly on the resource itself — like an S3 bucket policy allowing a specific role to read from it, with no role assumed
Emailing AWS support to manually request access for each service
There is no other pattern; role assumption is the only mechanism AWS supports
Disabling IAM entirely for the resource in question
questions.explain: Resource-based policies are a complementary pattern to role assumption — access granted directly by the resource, not via assuming a role.
